A board's analog input accepts $0$ to $3.3$ V and samples at whatever rate you
ask it to. Neither of those is automatically compatible with the signal you
actually want to measure: a generator's output is bipolar, and a signal fast
enough to be interesting is often fast enough to fold back on itself when
undersampled. This experiment builds the stage that reconciles the first
problem, demonstrates the second one deliberately, and then asks what a
filter — analog or digital — can and cannot do about it.

The central result is negative, and it is the one worth remembering:
**aliasing has to be prevented before the ADC samples, because nothing done
to the data afterward can undo it.** A folded component and a genuine signal
at the same apparent frequency produce identical samples; digital filtering
can clean up noise and interference that never folded, but it cannot tell the
two apart once they have.

## What you measure {#sec-s3-index-measure}

| Quantity | How | Where it is used later |
|---|---|---|
| Conditioning gain $G$ and offset $V_\mathrm{off}$ | Derived from the target ADC range, verified with a DMM at DC | Every voltage recovered from an S3 recording |
| Apparent frequency $f_a$ vs. predicted | A sweep of generator frequencies at one fixed, deliberately low $f_s$ | Confirms the folding relationship $f_a = \lvert f - k f_s\rvert$ |
| Anti-alias filter attenuation | Design computation, checked against the observed amplitude ratio of a filtered/unfiltered pair | Chooses $f_c$ and order for a required attenuation at a given $f_s$ |
| Digital filtering limits | FIR filtering of an oversampled run vs. an undersampled one | Shows why filtering cannot happen after the fact |

: What S3 produces {#tbl-s3-index-outputs}

## Bench {#sec-s3-index-bench}

**Tier 3.** A supported board, a signal generator capable of a bipolar output
and at least two simultaneous or sequential tones, a conditioning board (see
[the conditioning board](../../hardware/conditioning-board.qmd)), and a
filter stage (see [the anti-alias filter stage](../../hardware/filter-stage.qmd)).

**Board.** Any board with streaming support works; the aliasing sweep and the
filtered/unfiltered pair both need the sampling rate to be exactly what was
requested, which is the property S1 measured and S2 characterizes further.

**Host.** Linux is recommended, following the same evidence S1 gathered for
its own recommendation.

## Reference data {#sec-s3-index-data}

Nineteen generated runs ship with the experiment, in `data/`:

| File(s) | Contents |
|---|---|
| `alias-f0035` … `alias-f0935` (16 runs) | 2 s at 500 Hz each, one generator frequency per run, spanning $k = 0, 1, 2$ |
| `filter-off`, `filter-on` | 2 s at 500 Hz, a 650 Hz tone (aliases to 150 Hz) with no filter and with a 2-pole 100 Hz anti-alias filter |
| `oversampled` | 1 s at 5000 Hz, a 150 Hz signal plus a 1800 Hz interferer, nothing folded |

: Reference data shipped with S3 {#tbl-s3-index-data}

::: {.callout-warning}
## The reference data is synthetic

It is produced by a seeded generator (`tools/synth/s3_aliasing_filtering.py`)
whose parameters are plausible placeholders, not measurements — the
conditioning stage's and filter's own uncertainties in particular are marked
`TODO (Paolo)` in `tools/synth/params/s3.yaml`. It exists so the analysis
templates render, and are checked in continuous integration, with no bench
attached. Every page that uses it says so.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
## Instructor summary {.instructor-note}

Four hours, tier 3, needs S1 as a prerequisite — the conditioning-stage design
and the filter trade-off are where the session earns its extra hour over S1.
Full notes, expected values, common failures and the rubric are in the
[handbook](handbook.qmd#sec-s3-instructor).
:::
